summary: Defines a set of Diameter attribute-value pairs for describing how to classify traffic and what to do with it, such as filtering it or giving it a particular quality-of-service treatment. These building blocks can be reused by existing and future Diameter applications. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary:
Diameter is the protocol a network uses to check who is allowed on the network and what they get. This RFC adds a way to tell the network which traffic to treat in which way, using the same attribute format as the rest of Diameter.

A rule has two halves: a list of things to compare against each packet, and an action to take when a packet matches.

what are the treatment action values in diameter
subtitle: Diameter attributes that say which traffic to treat in which way, and how to treat it.

tldr.problem: Diameter already carried filtering and quality of service rules, but they were written in a loose free-text syntax borrowed from a firewall tool and could not match on Ethernet attributes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a set of attribute-value pairs in Diameter's own syntax: rule sets and rules, classifiers that match on addresses, ports and header fields, and actions that drop, shape, mark or permit the traffic that matches.
tldr.outcome: A network can now send a policy to a device in a form the device can read, and the attributes can be reused by existing and future Diameter applications. The document is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 5777 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It adds attributes to the Diameter base protocol defined in RFC 3588, and the QoS parameters it refers to are defined in RFC 5624. The signalling flows for a dedicated Diameter QoS application were still being specified elsewhere at the time of writing.

sections.title: Why Diameter Needs QoS Attributes
sections.content:
This document defines Diameter attribute-value pairs (AVPs) for classifying traffic and for the actions that filter it or give it a quality of service treatment. The AVPs can be used in existing and future Diameter applications, where the command extension policy of the application allows them.

The idea of sending quality of service information over Diameter goes back to the base protocol in RFC 3588. The filtering and QoS functionality was provided there by the IPFilterRule AVP and the QoSFilterRule AVP. Both relied on syntax taken from the FreeBSD ipfw tool, and the QoSFilterRule AVP was underspecified in RFC 3588 and later updated by RFC 4005.

This document replaces that approach. The goals are a uniform and extensible traffic classification mechanism written in Diameter's own syntax instead of free text, and an extensible set of actions that covers filtering and QoS treatment, so that the QoS functionality meets the needs of current networks.

The QoS-Resources AVP holds a complete rule set, with one Filter-Rule AVP per rule. Each rule has information for resolving conflicts between rules, a conditions part, and the actions to perform when those conditions are met. A rule can match all of the traffic or a subset of it, including traffic identified by Ethernet attributes, which the QoSFilterRule AVP could not do. Service differentiation can be based on Ethernet priority bits, a single layer of VLAN-IDs or stacked VLAN-IDs, Logical Link Control attributes, MAC addresses, or any combination of these. The header fields used for Ethernet classification come from the IEEE 802 series of specifications.

The policy rules are defined as Diameter encoded AVPs described using a modified version of ABNF, and the AVP data types are the ones from the base Diameter specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Diameter is the protocol a network uses to check who is allowed on the network and what they get. This RFC adds a way to tell the network which traffic to treat in which way, using the same attribute format as the rest of Diameter.

sections.title: Rule Sets, Rules and Their Order
sections.content:
The top-level element is the QoS-Resources AVP, code 508, of type Grouped, which holds a list of filter policy rules.

The Filter-Rule AVP, code 509, is also Grouped and defines one condition and action combination. It has four parts: an optional Filter-Rule-Precedence AVP for conflict resolution; the condition part, made of an optional Classifier AVP and any number of Time-Of-Day-Condition AVPs; the action part, made of an optional Treatment-Action AVP; and information about QoS related actions, made of optional QoS-Semantics, QoS-Profile-Template, QoS-Parameters and Excess-Treatment AVPs. Any number of other AVPs may be added as an extension point.

If the QoS-Profile-Template AVP is not included and the Treatment-Action AVP is set to shape or to mark, the default settings apply: the Vendor-Id AVP is set to 0, for IETF, and the QoS-Profile-Id AVP is set to zero, for the profile defined in RFC 5624. The contents of the QoS-Parameters AVP depend on the specification that defines those parameters; with the default vendor and profile identifiers, they are the AVPs defined in RFC 5624.

The Filter-Rule-Precedence AVP, code 510, of type Unsigned32, gives the execution order of the rules in the QoS-Resources AVP. The lower the number, the higher the precedence. Rules with equal precedence MAY be executed in parallel if the resource management function supports it. If the AVP is absent, the rules SHOULD be executed in the order in which they appear.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are held in one AVP, and each rule is another AVP inside it. Each rule says what to match and what to do. A number in each rule sets the order the rules run in, and lower numbers run first.

sections.title: Conditions: Classifiers and Time of Day
sections.content:
Two kinds of condition are introduced. Packet classification conditions are represented by the Classifier AVP, and time of day conditions by the Time-Of-Day-Condition AVP. If more than one Time-Of-Day-Condition AVP is present in a rule, the current time at rule evaluation MUST be within at least one of the time windows they specify. When both kinds of condition are present in the same rule, both must match for the action to be applied.

Classifiers are used in many applications to select a subset of data packets for subsequent treatment. In a QoS application, a packet that matches a classifier is treated in line with the QoS specification associated with that classifier. Figure 1 of the RFC shows a typical deployment: a managed terminal, the terminal the classifiers are for, on one side of a classifying entity, unmanaged terminals on the other side, and the AAA server that supplies the classifiers. The classifying entity classifies the packets arriving from the managed terminal and the packets leaving towards it.

A classifier is a group of attributes that specify how to match a packet. Each set of attributes gives values about aspects of the packet, typically its header, so different protocols use different attributes. In general a classifier has an identifier that uniquely identifies it and may be used to reference it from another structure; a From part that gives the rule for matching the source addresses; a To part that gives the rule for matching the destination addresses; a protocol that says which protocol is being matched; a direction that says whether the classifier applies to packets from the managed terminal, to it, or to both; and options, which are the attributes or properties of each protocol or layer and allow matching on those values. Each protocol type has its own set of attributes, grouped under the grouped Classifier AVP, code 511.

Time of day conditions are needed because in many QoS applications the treatment depends on when the flow was seen. The AVPs express one or more time windows during which a treatment action applies. They cover the time of day, the day of the week, the day of the month and the month of the year, either as recurring windows or as absolute start and end times, with a time zone flag and a time zone offset that ranges from -43200 to 43200 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: A rule can say two things about when it applies: which packets it matches, and what time it is. The packet part is a classifier, a list of things to compare against the packet header. The time part is a window, such as working hours on certain days.

sections.title: Matching Addresses and Ports
sections.content:
The From-Spec AVP, code 515, and the To-Spec AVP, code 516, are grouped AVPs that hold the source and the destination specifications used to match a packet. Each may appear any number of times in a classifier. If the From-Spec AVP is absent, all packets match regardless of the source address; the same holds for the destination and the To-Spec AVP. If more than one instance appears, the source of the packet can match any From-Spec AVP, and the destination can match any To-Spec AVP. The contents of these AVPs are protocol specific.

Both AVPs can hold the address and port AVPs: IP-Address, IP-Address-Range, IP-Address-Mask and Use-Assigned-Address for IP addresses; MAC-Address, MAC-Address-Mask, EUI64-Address and EUI64-Address-Mask for layer 2 addresses; and Port and Port-Range for ports. Within one of these groups, if the IP address AVPs appear then the source or destination IP address of the packet MUST match one of the addresses they represent. The same rule applies to the layer 2 address AVPs and to the port AVPs. If the IP address, MAC address and port AVPs all appear in the same From-Spec or To-Spec AVP, the packet MUST match all of the specifications: the IP address AND the MAC address AND the port number.

An IP-Address-Range AVP, code 519, holds an inclusive range, with an IP-Address-Start and an IP-Address-End address. A missing start means the range begins at the first valid address, and a missing end means it runs to the last one. For the range to be valid the start MUST be less than the end. An IP-Address-Mask AVP, code 522, gives a base address and the bit width of the mask, so a range written as 192.0.2.0/24 matches every address from 192.0.2.0 up to and including 192.0.2.255.

A Negated AVP, code 517, of type Enumerated with the values True and False, inverts the match: when it is True the classifier matches addresses other than those specified, and when it is False, or absent, it matches the addresses specified. The RFC notes that the negation does not affect the port comparisons.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side of the packet can be matched on its IP address, its hardware address and its port number. You can give a single address, a range, or a network expressed as a base address and a prefix length. A negation flips the match, so the rule applies to everything except the addresses you listed.

sections.title: Matching on Header and Ethernet Fields
sections.content:
Besides addresses and ports, a classifier can match on the header fields of the protocols in use. The Classifier AVP can hold the Diffserv-Code-Point AVP, code 535, which matches the Diffserv codepoint, and the Fragmentation-Flag AVP, code 536, which matches the fragmentation flag of the IP header.

Options can be matched too. The IP-Option AVP, code 537, holds an IP-Option-Type and an IP-Option-Value. The TCP-Option AVP, code 540, holds a TCP-Option-Type and a TCP-Option-Value. The TCP-Flags AVP, code 543, is a grouped AVP holding the TCP flag types to match, and the ICMP-Type AVP, code 545, holds an ICMP type number and an ICMP code.

Ethernet has AVPs of its own. The ETH-Option AVP, code 548, is grouped and holds the ETH-Proto-Type AVP together with any number of VLAN-ID-Range and User-Priority-Range AVPs. The ETH-Proto-Type AVP, code 549, specifies the encapsulated protocol type, using either the ETH-Ether-Type AVP, code 550, which carries the Ethertype field of the packet to match, or the ETH-SAP AVP, code 551, which carries the 802.2 service access point, with the destination and source SAP in the two octets. The two are mutually exclusive.

A VLAN-ID-Range AVP, code 552, matches the VLAN identity, either a single VLAN-ID as in IEEE 802.1Q or a combination of customer and service VLAN-IDs as in IEEE 802.1ad. A single VLAN-ID is expressed with the C-VID-Start and C-VID-End AVPs, and the S-VID AVPs are then omitted. The start and end values MUST be in the range from 0 to 4095. If the range AVPs are omitted from the classifier, the VLAN identity of the packet is not compared at all.

The User-Priority-Range AVP, code 557, matches the user_priority parameter of IEEE 802.1D. A packet matches when its value is at least the Low-User-Priority and at most the High-User-Priority, both of which MUST be in the range from 0 to 7.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule can also look inside the headers: the service class byte, the fragmentation flag, IP and TCP options, TCP flags, ICMP types, and for Ethernet the protocol type, the VLAN tags and the priority bits.

sections.title: Actions and QoS Semantics
sections.content:
The action part of a rule says what to do with traffic that matches. The Treatment-Action AVP, code 572, is an Enumerated AVP with four values defined in this document.

  • 0: drop. The traffic MUST be dropped.
  • 1: shape. Shaping is, in the words of RFC 2475, the process of delaying packets within a traffic stream to cause it to conform to some defined traffic profile. The QoS-Parameters AVP SHALL then contain QoS information AVPs, such as the TMOD-1 and Bandwidth AVPs of RFC 5624, that say how to shape the traffic.
  • 2: mark. Marking is, in the words of RFC 2475, the process of setting the DS codepoint in a packet based on defined rules. The QoS-Parameters AVP SHALL then contain QoS information AVPs, such as the PHB-Class AVP of RFC 5624, that say which Diffserv marking to apply.
  • 3: permit. This is the counterpart of drop, and allows traffic that matches the condition to bypass.

RFC 2475 also describes policing, the process of discarding packets within a traffic stream in accordance with the state of a meter enforcing a traffic profile. The RFC models that behaviour in the rule itself, by including the Excess-Treatment AVP with a Treatment-Action AVP set to drop. Further action values can be registered later.

The QoS-Profile-Template AVP, code 574, is grouped and gives the namespace of the QoS profile, through the Vendor-Id AVP with a 32-bit IANA Private Enterprise Number, and the specific profile, through the QoS-Profile-Id AVP, code 573, of type Unsigned32. A vendor identifier of zero is used for IETF, and the initial QoS profile template has the value zero and is defined in RFC 5624.

The QoS-Semantics AVP, code 575, says what the profile and the parameters in the rule mean. It has five values: QoS-Desired, QoS-Available, QoS-Delivered, Minimum-QoS and QoS-Authorized. QoS-Desired from the client to the server asks for that QoS to be authorized. QoS-Available in the direction from client to server means admission control at the client says the QoS is available, and in the other direction it means admission control at the server says it is available. QoS-Delivered from client to server is the client reporting the QoS actually delivered to the terminal. Minimum-QoS from client to server says the client is not interested in authorizing QoS lower than that, and in the other direction that the client must not be given guarantees lower than that. QoS-Authorized from the server to the client is the server authorizing that QoS.

The QoS-Parameters AVP, code 576, is grouped and carries the QoS parameters themselves, which are defined in separate documents and depend on the profile template. The Excess-Treatment AVP, code 577, is grouped and says how out-of-profile traffic is treated, that is traffic not covered by the profile template and the parameters. It carries a Treatment-Action AVP and, optionally, a profile template and parameters of its own. If the Excess-Treatment AVP is absent, the treatment of out-of-profile traffic is left to the node doing the QoS treatment.
sections.plainLanguage: The action part says what happens to matching traffic: drop it, shape it to a traffic profile, mark it with a service class, or let it pass. A separate part says how the traffic that goes beyond the profile is treated, which is how rate policing is expressed.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives several signalling flows where quality of service is negotiated inside ordinary Diameter applications.

In the EAP example, a Network Access Server announces its QoS awareness and capabilities in the Diameter-EAP-Request message, and once the EAP exchange is complete the Diameter server returns a pre-provisioned QoS profile, with the QoS-Semantics set to QoS-Authorized, in the final Diameter-EAP-Answer. The NASREQ example does the same with the NASREQ application.

In the authorization-only example the NAS sends the Diameter server a QoS-Resources AVP with the QoS-Semantics set to QoS-Desired. The server either authorizes the QoS or rejects it and tells the NAS the result, answering with a QoS-Resources AVP whose semantics are QoS-Authorized. In this case the NAS does not need to send the QoS-Capability AVP, because the QoS-Resources AVP implies the same thing, and because the NAS is asking about one specific profile rather than a pre-provisioned one.

The server-initiated re-authorization example has the Diameter server send a Re-Auth Request for an existing session, which the NAS acknowledges. The NAS then starts the same re-authorization procedure for the QoS profile it already holds.

In the credit control example the client asks for a QoS authorization in the initial Credit Control Request, the server answers with the granted resources and an authorized QoS definition, and at the end of the service the client reports the units used and the QoS level at which they were delivered, with the semantics set to QoS-Delivered.

Two classifier examples show the syntax in use. The first classifies packets from hosts on the subnet 192.0.2.0/24 to ports 80, 8090 or 443 on three web servers, using an IP-Address-Mask with a bit width of 24 for the source and a list of IP addresses and ports for the destination. The second matches SIP signalling traffic from a device with a given MAC address to servers in the address range 192.0.2.90 to 192.0.2.190.

The QoS parameter examples show how the AVPs interwork with the parameters of RFC 5624. A rule that limits traffic to 1 Mbit/s and drops out-of-profile traffic needs the Treatment-Action set to shape, the QoS-Parameters AVP carrying the Bandwidth AVP with the 1 Mbit/s limit, and the Treatment-Action inside the Excess-Treatment AVP set to drop. A second example marks in-profile traffic of 5 Mbit/s with one PHB class and out-of-profile traffic with another, using the Treatment-Action set to mark, a TMOD-1 AVP and a PHB-Class AVP in the QoS-Parameters AVP, and an Excess-Treatment AVP carrying a second PHB-Class AVP.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show how the attributes appear in real exchanges: a server handing a profile to a network access server, a client asking for a QoS and getting it authorized, and a client reporting what it actually delivered.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document describes an extension of Diameter for conveying quality of service information. The security considerations of the Diameter protocol itself are discussed in RFC 3588. Use of the AVPs defined here MUST take into account the security issues and requirements of the Diameter base protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new here. The security rules of the Diameter base protocol apply to these attributes as well.
